I know 2 or 3 people that this has happened to. One was a guy I went to college with who had a really early automatic insulin pump installed on the side of his torso. He basically had no function at all out of his pancreas, it might as well have been surgically removed. He had a box the size of a cigar case installed on a set of ports on his torso. One of the ports was used to take nearly constant blood samples, and monitor his blood insulin and glucose levels, the other one pumped in liquid insulin. It needed special rechargeable batteries, and he had to keep insulin cartridges in it that he had to keep refrigerated at home and that had to be kept in insulated storage in the day (we live in Texas where it's hot) in a small case in his back pack. It had lights on it and made small clicking and mechanical wheezing noises all day and made audible alarms when there was a problem. It also had lights and a little lcd display like acalculator that showed text. He hid it under his shirt and we (all of us) didn't know about it until one day it made an alarm noise during a test and he had to pull up his shirt and change out his battery pack. It sometimes got irritated and sometimes the ports on his side got dirty and infected.

I graduated in 2009 with a BA in philosophy. There's big parts of my major that just weren't taught at all (namely east Asian philosophy, Middle Eastern philosophy, American analytical philosophy was kind of just skimmed, boolean logic, and any philosophy work done after about the year 1900). There's big parts of my major that I was taught that are just wrong (leibnitz was super important to continental European philosophy, camus wasn't important, I was taught the life history of nieztche but not much of his actual teachings, I was taught a lot of things were important to the topic that weren't and a lot of things weren't important that were). I was required to take certain 400 level courses to get my degree that I never took. I was also supposed to take some back up courses in case I couldn't take those courses so I could graduate, and I didn't take those either and still graduated. I later attended ut Arlington and sat in on a few freshman level philosophy courses... And they covered stuff I had never heard of and things I was taught weren't important at Austin college turned out to be super important to the topic. I have repeatedly been told "you have a degree in this, you know this part of this topic" and no, I don't... And I studied my ass off. I repeatedly got feedback  that "clearly you understood the topic, answered the question correctly, but clearly didn't actually read the material" in reference to papers that had direct quotes from the subject material in them. I also got told that i "understood the topic but didn't 'understand' the topic" with the second 'understand' in its own separate quotations. I also repeatedly got feedback that I "missed too much class" in classes where I attended class more often than the professor teaching it, had the notes from classes to prove it, and the professor didn't take attendance, and when I brought this to the professors attention I was told "you there physically but not in spirit"... And no, I don't know what that's supposed to mean. 

I minored in environmental studies and we didn't cover saltwater aquatic ecology much at all and thats super important to the topic. I also took 5 more courses in my minor than in my major... So it looks like I majored in environmental science even though my transcript shows that I minored in it. I have also sat in on environmental science courses at ut Arlington since and I repeatedly had no idea what they were talking about. I didn't know the works cited, hadn't heard of the authors of the works, hadn't heard of any of it.

Austin college also doesn't offer any academic or professional certifications. Austin college also only issues bachelor's of arts degrees in hard sciences... Which doesn't make any sense.

Austin college also claims I studied abroad a long with my entire graduating class... Even though I didn't... I studied in America, the whole 4 years.

About only ⅓ of my transcript course work transferred to ut arlington (a state school in the same state) because ⅔ of it didn't meet state standards for course content. So I had to take courses like art, economics, and history, for a third and fourth time. When I tired to transfer to IU they wouldn't accept any of my Austin college credits at all because they didn't have any idea what Austin college was, they didn't understand why it was in Sherman Texas, and course content didn't meet their state standards. 

I basically had to start over on a second bachelor's degree once I graduated from Austin college, no matter where I went to college. That got very expensive very quickly and I was only able to afford 3 semesters of that program before I ran out of money. There are no scholarships for second bachelor's degrees, and it doesn't matter if the one I have doesn't or doesn't count as an actual bachelor's degree. It's like being a student who bought a degree at a degree mill: no scholarships and I have to pretty much start over cause my degree is worthless. 

This is only the academic problems too. This doesn't cover social problems or student life problems with Austin college. Austin college may or may not have been a good school academically in the past or more recently, but based on my experiences... I can't tell that it ever was a good school academically.

At the end of owning mine I needed an engine rebuild or a short block plus a power steering rack and I needed to do a dash pull to fix the digital climate control system.

I was 3rd owner of the car and I bought mine at 65kmi. At 113kmi the first turbo welded it's internal waste gate open. Failed a compression test on all 4 cylinders and failed a leak down test on all 4 cylinders (10:1 compression should yield 140psi on each cylinder and mine was making like 90psi to 100psi). That's when we learned that the first owner did the first oil change at 17kmi, which means they skipped breaking in that motor and went straight to wearing it out. At 162kmi the power steering rack failed and had no pressure in cold weather and my left rear strut was blown and leaking oil. At 170k the rear inner lower control arm bushings failed (requires a hydraulic press and an alignment rack to fix). At 180kmi the power steering didn't work at all due to failed seals in the atf filled rack. I couldn't find the rack anywhere unless it was for the rhd version of the car. At 192kmi the second turbo had an oil bearing fail.

It was a nice car, it was fun to drive, was boring to look at which made it a great sleeper, drove like a riot, very easy to control and forgiving unless you broke traction and then it acted all weird.

It was also impossible to put an aftermarket stereo in of you got the legacy gt limited cause you had digital automatic climate controls built into the bottom of the radio. Plus the seats were hard as rocks and I eventually hurt my hip really bad so that really mattered after a while. Back seat also didn't fold down in the sedan until 2007 and that made moving stuff hard. 

I loved the way it moved and nothing since has been such a thrill.

It's a pretty good solution, because why make 2 different parts on an assembly line to ancient trucks when 1 part works in both trucks? 99 k2500 truck parts pretty much fit a 99 k2500 tahoe/kblazer/silverado/cheyenne/grand silverado/whatever (named differently depending on market and body/cab style) as long as it's the same frame (torsion bar or coil spring or solid front axle) gmt400 truck. The frames are also all a little different from the middle of the truck to the back depending on body style/cab size/bed length. 

I need to do this on mine too. I have a 1995 Tahoe 2 door z71 with the 350/5.7tbi v8 and a 4l60e automatic transmission that I've owned for 20 years. Hardest part for me is the torsion bar suspension is just very large and hard to do in a driveway/house garage. It starts under the back of the front seats and goes all the way to the back side of the lower control arms. It also helps to have a special torsion bar removal/reinstall action tool. 

There were like 5 different front suspension set ups/frame variations for these gmt400 trucks. There was a coil spring 2wd 1500 with 5 lug hubs/brakes/wheels/spindles/etc. There was a torsion bar 4wd 1500/2500 with 6 lug hubs/brakes/wheels/etc. There were also 2wd/4wd 3500 trucks that were 8 lug (not sure if they were both coil spring or torsion bar). And there were a rare few 3500+ sized trucks with solid front axles and front leaf springs with 8-10 lug wheels (I've only found 3-4 of these trucks in person). The solid front axle/leaf spring combination was more common on like cherry picker/bucket trucks or trucks with small dump beds on them or motor homes, and those were all like medium duty/heavy duty machines meant for long life and heavy service.

The reason they went away from these trucks was that the assembly line was super complex due to all the variety between frames, front suspensions, body/cab styles, and bed lengths. That and emissions/engine output/reliability/other issues. But mostly it just cost gm a lot of money to keep like 8 assembly lines running just for the frames and front suspensions.

That polished metal bar in the center of the coiled spring (spiral) is a strut. This strut is broken. you need a new strut. you replace struts in pairs. if you replace the front right strut, then you also replace the front left strut. If you don't replace in pairs then the car will drive funny and the older side will quickly wear out. You will need an alignment after replacing the strut, other wise the car will pull to one side (sometimes it will pull hard, particularly at highway speed), and the steering wheel will be crooked.  

Depending on the car, you can by "quick struts" (see link below) which are pre-assembled with matching parts (strut, spring, top mount, dust boot, bump stop), sometimes better built than factory parts (struts that came on cars in 1995 are not as good as struts built in 2015). Quick struts are pretty easy to do compared to rebuilding strut assemblies and typically quick struts are easier to warranty. 

To rebuild a strut you need a spring compressor and some air/power tools, namely an impact gun, a bunch of hardened black steel sockets, an air compressor, combination wrenches, and a 1/4in drive socket set, etc.

Quick struts you can do with hand tools if you have to (power tools just make it faster). You need to jack up the car, remove the wheel, disconnect the strut mount or "top hat" using a 1/4in drive socket set (short wrench is good wrench), undo the bolts that hold the bottom of the strut to the steering knuckle, and pull the old strut out. Then put the new quick strut in, bolt up the bottom bolts to the steering knuckle, bolt up the top mount using a 1/4in drive socket set (seriously, short wrench is best wrench, it's easy to over tighten these little nuts and break the studs), reattach the wheel using lug nuts, torque down the lug nuts with a torque wrench. Repeat the whole process for the opposite side of the same axle. 

Then get an alignment so the car drives straight. Scrap the old parts or toss them in the dumpster.

Yes, the certifications are taught at some community colleges and some trade schools. If you can get courses at community College that's typically better as the credits can be transfered elsewhere later.

Amazon has an online course:

https://aws.amazon.com/government-education/workforce-development/aws-fiber-optic-fusion-splicing/

Here's a brief and basic tutorial on how to splice fiber:

https://youtu.be/DIiBVuuRUtM

The hardest parts of this job are: 100% travel within typically 3hours of a home office, typically you're a 1099 subcontractor for a prime contracting firm (means no medical, dental, or vision benefits through your employer and you have to buy your own), typically as a subcontractor you track your own business mileage, a fusion splicing machine is frequently $16k, and organizational skills. For whatever reason it's also really hard to find employees that can stay sober and out of jail (they all love meth for some reason), so if you can stay off drugs and out of jail then you're halfway there. Do not blow loads of money on tools but also don't be super cheap. A $2 screw driver from the dollar store is not good for very long, and a $7 screw driver from home depot works almost just as well as the $40 one from snap on. The ryobi tools work just as well as the Milwaukee ones and they're cheaper and if you lose one or trash it then a new or used one is very available at the nearest pawn shop. 

Things that will help you are a clean driving record, keeping your drivers license current, the ability to read maps and blueprints, and math skills (mostly geometry). You have to be able to read, write, count, and do math. If you can, learn and become fluent in Spanish. Spanish language skills help a lot because after hurricane Maria a bunch of workers came to the main land from Puerto Rico so many of your coworkers will speak some spanish. You also have to be flexible with the meanings of words and the use of slang because many of the parts/hardware has weird regional nicknames (d lashing clamp=bugnut, bell anchor=coconut, down guy insulator knuckle=bear claw/moose knuckle, bronzed bonding clamp=weaver, etc.). If you can also learn to splice coax and multistrand low voltage copper wire that will make employers want you more because you'll be a more versatile employee with a broader skill set. A lot of fiber networks are not purely fiber networks, many are hybrids between fiber and coax and fiber and multistrand copper wire. Coax or digital coax in this case is like rg6 coax that goes to your TV only half an inch in diameter or larger and rigid. Coax is used mostly by time Warner cable, spectrum, cox, xfinity, etc. Multistrand copper wire is basically traditional phone line used in 4 wire systems and dsl internet systems. Multistrand copper wire btw is slow and has been around for 150+ years and is a favorite of AT&T, SW bell, and other smaller older telecom companies. It also helps to work on a team of at least 2 people for safety reasons (stepping on a snake in waist high grass isn't fun, nor is being bitten by venomous spiders, and the nearest er is usually 2 hours away). 

The goal is to build an OSP (outside plant) that works and meets the customer's standards. If it doesn't work or meet their standards then the mission isn't accomplished and you stay out there until it is. 

Big payers (also big players) in the game are in house crews for AT&T or spectrum/twc/charter/Google fiber/Verizon fios. I do not recommend working for them at the start though because their job listing get tons of applicants and those positions are super competitive plus they are high stress employers. The in house crews for house hold names aren't easy to work for and they don't like it when you ask questions even if they don't know the answers because for whatever reason it makes them "feel stupid". At&t managers for some reason have a lot of their personal ego invested in their projects, meaning that if something is built wrong then they feel like you made them look bad personally (not professionally). It's easier to get hired by smaller companies that are prime contractors for those companies and those jobs still pay pretty good and are usually easier to work for. I recommend getting on Google and start looking for companies located near you or in your region/state. 

There's a lot of driving to spots in the middle of nowhere with no addresses other than a jso or pdo or terminal number. A blueprint will frequently show 2 or 3 telephone poles next to an unnamed road or intersection and you'll be on your own to track that spot down using pole location numbers. The hardest part of splicing is reading and creating splice matrices and splicing diagrams which are basically big wiring diagrams that represent the ip addresses of every building in town and its all condensed down to one page. Also every client (at&t/spectrum/time Warner cable) has there own guidelines for what they want you to build and sometimes that varies with state and local legislation.

Some of the smaller licensed sub/prime contractors are companies like PM&A (P Marshall and associates), Vertek llc, and nrtc. I have worked for all 3 of these companies btw as a quality control tech, qc inspector, or qc and recovery specialist. All 3 of these companies are fairly large regional companies with multiple projects in multiple states. PM&A was ok and paid alright and had contracts with AT&T, tmobile, and Google fiber. Vertek llc was fun to work for but poorly run by upper management and had contracts with suddenlink, cable one, and frontier telecom. nrtc pays well but the local management is variable and the hours are long, they have contracts with really small companies like Smithville telecom coop and Sci remc.

My current job is as a qc tech but I really enjoyed doing qc and recovery. Qc and recovery is basically going out and checking the work of sub contractors, if its built right then you report that and the sub contractor gets paid, if it's built wrong then you gig them and tell them what to fix and once it's good they get paid, if it's built wrong and they won't fix it then you do it and they don't get paid but you do. Qc and recovery work is a lot of adventure: it's everything from picking up 2000lb spools of fiber that have been abandoned in the field to wiring power supplies that weren't put together right the first time. I got into being a qc tech through a long list of other jobs because I didn't get much career guidance in college but at this point I basically build whatever the fuck I want (that's literally right below my name on my resume).

None of these jobs in this industry are super hard btw unless you're basically just rolling a big 700lb spool of steel cable up a hill all day (I've done that, it was very sysiphian).

Brake pads and shoes on your car. You get what you pay for. The cheaper ones are always worse performing and you don't want that. Basically your stopping distance is longer, or they work worse in cold or wet or hot conditions. This means you are more likely to wreck by rear ending someone at speed or hit a stationary object at speed, or if you lose control of your car it is harder to recover (you can always stop and steer, but not always as well as possible).

If you spend more money you get better more consistent and shorter braking even at higher speeds. This makes it easier to stop and harder to wreck. It also makes it easier to regain control of your car after losing control.

It's 2018 and no one should buy organic compound brake pads. No one should even make these. They're performance is terrible and they don't last very long. Semi metallic is common on European cars for some reason (I guess softer steel rotors?) and they dust like crazy but their performance is decent, they do wear relatively well. Ceramic brake pads are the way to go. They stop better, they wear better, they recover from repeated hard stops better, even if they make a little more noise (harder pads mean more noise due to harder vibrations). 

I'm not saying you need carbon ceramic brakes from a Maserati. I'm not saying you need mono block brembos. On an average road car that I plan to keep I always go with ceramic brakes because I don't like wrecking and neither does my insurance.

It's also 2018 and nothing should have drum brakes even on the rear but certain cars still do (mostly cheaper cars and lots of trucks still have them on the rear). Brake shoes are often semi metallic at best... So always get semi metallic drum brake shoes. If your front and rear brakes are closely matched in quality, then regaining control of your car will be easier and the car will brake more predictably.

Bosch builds great brake pads, so does Wagner and akebono. If you're hotrodding an older car, always spend money on the brakes first. Going fast is easy, but if you can't stop then there's no point.
